sourceCheck: Verified the official guide, all four domain pages and their numbered skills, Revisions, both service-scope pages, and the certification exam page. Revisions identifies guide version 2.1, published December 12, 2024; each task has a single numbered Skill list. All 13 task titles and the 32%/26%/24%/18% domain weights match the supplied sections. DVA-C02 remains available. The exam page announces DVA-C03 registration on October 27, 2026, but now gives December 1, 2026 as DVA-C02's last testing day, differing from the supplied November 30 date. It still links the DVA-C02 guide, defers DVA-C03 preparation resources to October 27, and does not state a DVA-C03 delivery start date; no published DVA-C03 guide was found. This deck follows DVA-C02. The SDK retry reference was opened and its AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026 opt-in notice checked; the retry cards avoid SDK-specific defaults and numerical retry settings.

cards.statement: Amazon SNS supports delivering a published message to several subscribed Amazon SQS queues.
cards.explanation: SNS sends a separate copy to subscribed queues, allowing their consumers to process the same publication independently.

source.title: Fanout Amazon SNS notifications to Amazon SQS queues for asynchronous processing

cards.statement: For a state with Retry and Catch, AWS Step Functions evaluates Catch before Retry.
cards.explanation: Step Functions checks Retry first. It evaluates Catch after retry handling is exhausted or the error has no applicable retrier.
cards.misconception: Catch handlers take priority over retry rules.

source.title: Handling errors in Step Functions workflows

cards.statement: Amazon SQS deletes a message as soon as ReceiveMessage returns it to a consumer.
cards.explanation: Receiving an SQS message leaves it in the queue. The consumer sends a separate delete request after processing it.
cards.misconception: Receiving a message acknowledges it and removes it from the queue.

source.title: Receiving and deleting a message in Amazon SQS

cards.statement: An Amazon SQS FIFO queue preserves send order across messages with different MessageGroupId values.
cards.explanation: SQS FIFO ordering applies within a message group. Messages in different groups can be processed out of order relative to one another.
cards.misconception: FIFO ordering spans the entire queue across message groups.

source.title: FIFO queue delivery logic in Amazon SQS

cards.statement: Amazon API Gateway REST API request validation supports checking header values against a JSON schema.
cards.explanation: REST API request validation checks required headers for presence and nonblank values. JSON schema validation applies to the request body.
cards.misconception: Request models validate header formats in the same way as request bodies.

source.title: Request validation for REST APIs in API Gateway

cards.statement: An Amazon API Gateway REST API can select a request mapping template using the request's Content-Type.
cards.explanation: For REST API mapping template transformations, API Gateway matches Content-Type to the configured templates and evaluates the matching template for the request payload.

source.title: Mapping template transformations for REST APIs in API Gateway

cards.statement: AWS SDK standard retry mode adds jitter to backoff delays to spread retry attempts over time.
cards.explanation: Jitter randomizes AWS SDK retry timing, reducing synchronized retry bursts from clients recovering from the same failure.

cards.statement: An AWS SDK client in adaptive retry mode can send its initial request before checking the rate limiter.
cards.explanation: Adaptive mode checks its client-side rate limiter before sending the initial request, so throttling can delay that request.
cards.misconception: Adaptive mode rate-limits retry attempts but exempts the initial request.

cards.statement: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams can select a shard by hashing a record's PartitionKey.
cards.explanation: For partition-key routing, Kinesis hashes PartitionKey and finds the shard whose hash range contains that hash.

source.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Terminology and concepts

cards.statement: Amazon EventBridge PutEvents reports entry-level failures through a failed HTTP response.
cards.explanation: PutEvents can return an HTTP success response containing failed entries. The caller checks FailedEntryCount and the error details in Entries.
cards.misconception: An HTTP success response means that EventBridge accepted the entire batch.

cards.statement: Amazon EventBridge ignores event fields omitted from an event pattern when checking for a match.
cards.explanation: An EventBridge pattern constrains the fields it includes. Extra event fields can vary while the event still matches.

cards.statement: AWS Step Functions resumes a waiting callback task when SendTaskSuccess supplies its matching task token.
cards.explanation: The worker sends the task token with its result. Step Functions uses that callback to finish the paused task and continue the execution.

source.title: Discover service integration patterns in Step Functions

cards.statement: AWS Lambda assigns a public IPv4 address to a function connected to a public VPC subnet.
cards.explanation: A public subnet attachment gives a Lambda function no public IPv4 address. The subnet's route to an internet gateway alone does not provide IPv4 internet access.
cards.misconception: Selecting a public subnet makes a Lambda function publicly addressed like an EC2 instance.

source.title: Giving Lambda functions access to resources in an Amazon VPC

cards.statement: Lambda passes an environment variable's configured value to function code as a literal string.
cards.explanation: Lambda leaves variable references unexpanded. If a value refers to another variable, your code performs that evaluation.

cards.statement: A Lambda on-success destination receives the function's result inside an invocation record.
cards.explanation: Lambda puts the returned value in responsePayload, alongside information about the asynchronous invocation.

source.title: Capturing records of Lambda asynchronous invocations

cards.statement: A Lambda SQS handler can list failed message IDs in batchItemFailures for a partial batch response.
cards.explanation: Enable ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping and return failed IDs as itemIdentifier entries. Lambda then retries the failed messages.

source.title: Handling errors for an SQS event source in Lambda

cards.statement: AWS Lambda Invoke returns an HTTP error status when a synchronous handler throws an exception.
cards.explanation: A synchronous Invoke handler failure appears in FunctionError and the response payload. The HTTP status reflects the invocation request's success.
cards.misconception: A function exception makes the synchronous Invoke API request fail at the HTTP level.

cards.statement: Lambda reserved concurrency prepares execution environments before incoming invocations.
cards.explanation: Reserved concurrency sets aside and caps concurrent execution capacity. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes environments to reduce cold starts.
cards.misconception: Reserved concurrency prewarms environments to prevent cold starts.

source.title: Configuring reserved concurrency for a function

cards.statement: AWS Lambda retains /tmp files when it reuses the same execution environment for another invocation.
cards.explanation: The /tmp directory survives an execution environment's freeze and reuse. Code can reuse cached files while that environment remains available.

source.title: Understanding the Lambda execution environment lifecycle

cards.statement: Lambda functions packaged as container images can load dependencies from attached Lambda layers.
cards.explanation: Lambda layers attach to functions packaged as .zip archives. A container image includes its dependencies during the image build.
cards.misconception: Container image functions attach layers in the same way as .zip functions.

cards.statement: Increasing a Lambda function's configured memory also increases its allocated CPU resources.
cards.explanation: Lambda allocates CPU power in proportion to configured memory, so memory tuning also changes the compute available to the code.

cards.statement: Lambda supports reusing an SDK client initialized outside the handler across invocations in the same environment.
cards.explanation: An SDK client created during initialization survives warm invocations in that environment, avoiding repeated client setup.

source.title: Best practices for working with AWS Lambda functions

cards.statement: A Lambda event source mapping for Amazon Kinesis Data Streams passes a record as the handler's top-level event.
cards.explanation: Lambda wraps Kinesis records in a Records array in the event passed to the handler, allowing the handler to process a batch.
cards.misconception: The Kinesis trigger passes an individual record as the complete event object.

source.title: Using Lambda to process records from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

cards.statement: Lambda runs an event source mapping's FilterCriteria evaluation inside the function handler.
cards.explanation: The Lambda service evaluates event source mapping filters before invoking the function. The handler receives records that pass those filters.
cards.misconception: FilterCriteria is a filter that Lambda applies inside the handler at runtime.

source.title: Control which events Lambda sends to your function

cards.statement: A DynamoDB Query uses equality on the partition key in its KeyConditionExpression.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB Query targets a specified partition key value. Its key condition supplies that value through an equality comparison.

source.title: Key condition expressions for the Query operation in DynamoDB

cards.statement: A DynamoDB Query FilterExpression reduces the read capacity consumed by the request.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB applies FilterExpression after reading the items, so filtering changes the returned results rather than the read capacity consumed.
cards.misconception: Filtering unwanted items reduces the read capacity charged for a Query.

source.title: Filter expressions for the Query operation in DynamoDB

cards.statement: DynamoDB supports strongly consistent Query requests against global secondary indexes.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB global secondary indexes provide eventually consistent reads. A Query requesting strong consistency on a GSI is rejected.
cards.misconception: The ConsistentRead option works on global secondary indexes as it does on tables.

cards.statement: DynamoDB PutItem can use attribute_not_exists to protect an existing item from replacement.
cards.explanation: A PutItem condition using attribute_not_exists on the partition key fails when an item with that primary key already exists.

cards.statement: DynamoDB BatchWriteItem can finish the writes listed in UnprocessedItems after it returns its response.
cards.explanation: BatchWriteItem returns unfinished operations in UnprocessedItems. Application code resubmits those operations in a later request.
cards.misconception: BatchWriteItem completes retryable item failures after returning its response.

cards.statement: DynamoDB removes expired items from read results as soon as their TTL timestamp passes.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB deletes TTL-expired items asynchronously. Reads can return expired items while they await deletion.
cards.misconception: An expired TTL timestamp immediately hides an item from DynamoDB reads.

source.title: Using time to live (TTL) in DynamoDB

cards.statement: The DynamoDB low-level API sends an N attribute's numeric value as a string.
cards.explanation: The N tag identifies a number even though its wire value is a string. DynamoDB still treats the stored attribute numerically.

cards.statement: An Amazon S3 GetObject call for the current version reflects a successfully completed object overwrite.
cards.explanation: Amazon S3 makes successful object overwrites visible to subsequent reads through strong read-after-write consistency.

cards.statement: Amazon S3 DeleteObject with a key alone permanently removes existing versions in a versioning-enabled bucket.
cards.explanation: In a versioning-enabled bucket, DeleteObject with a key alone creates a delete marker. Existing object versions remain stored.
cards.misconception: Deleting an object key erases its stored versions even when versioning is enabled.

cards.statement: In ElastiCache for Redis OSS, EXPIRE sets a lifetime for the whole hash stored under a key.
cards.explanation: EXPIRE attaches a timer to the hash's key. When that key expires, Redis OSS removes the hash and its fields.

cards.statement: Amazon RDS Data API commits an ExecuteStatement change when the caller omits transactionId.
cards.explanation: An ExecuteStatement call with transactionId absent runs outside an explicit Data API transaction. RDS Data API commits changes from that call.

cards.statement: Amazon OpenSearch Service analyzes a term query's input using the target field's text analyzer.
cards.explanation: An OpenSearch term query compares its input as an exact term rather than analyzing it as full text. Input should match the indexed term.
cards.misconception: A term query analyzes its input like a full-text match query.

cards.statement: An Amazon Cognito user pool issues AWS access keys after a user signs in.
cards.explanation: Cognito user pool sign-in returns JSON web tokens for application authentication and authorization, rather than AWS access keys.
cards.misconception: Cognito user pool sign-in supplies credentials for direct AWS API calls.

cards.statement: An Amazon Cognito access token uses a different signing key than the ID token from the same session.
cards.explanation: Cognito signs access and ID tokens with separate keys. Code selects the verification key from the token's kid value.

cards.statement: An Amazon API Gateway HTTP API JWT authorizer checks a present aud claim against its configured audience.
cards.explanation: For an HTTP API, API Gateway compares the JWT's aud value with the authorizer's audience entries to check the token's intended recipient.

source.title: Control access to HTTP APIs with JWT authorizers in API Gateway

cards.statement: Setting apiKeyRequired on an Amazon API Gateway REST API method enables IAM authorization for that method.
cards.explanation: apiKeyRequired enables REST API key enforcement. The method's authorizationType setting selects its authorization mechanism.
cards.misconception: Enabling required API keys also turns on IAM request authorization.

cards.statement: An explicit Deny in an applicable IAM policy overrides an Allow for the same request.
cards.explanation: AWS rejects a request covered by an applicable explicit Deny even when another applicable policy grants that access.

cards.statement: An IAM permissions boundary can grant actions through its own Allow statements.
cards.explanation: A permissions boundary limits permissions available to an IAM entity. Its Allow statements set a ceiling rather than grant access.
cards.misconception: A permissions boundary grants permissions like an attached identity policy.

cards.statement: AWS STS AssumeRole returns temporary credentials that include a session token.
cards.explanation: AssumeRole returns an access key ID, secret access key and session token. Code supplies that token when using the temporary credentials.

cards.statement: AWS STS GetCallerIdentity can return the original IAM user's ARN for a request using assumed-role credentials.
cards.explanation: With assumed-role credentials, GetCallerIdentity returns the assumed-role session's ARN. It identifies the active session rather than the IAM user who assumed the role.
cards.misconception: Assuming a role leaves GetCallerIdentity reporting the original IAM user.

cards.statement: AWS Signature Version 4 sends the caller's secret access key with the signed API request.
cards.explanation: SigV4 derives a signing key from the secret access key and sends a calculated signature. The secret access key stays with the signer.
cards.misconception: SigV4 transmits the secret access key so AWS can authenticate the request.

source.title: Create a signed AWS API request

cards.statement: A caller passing an execution role to AWS Lambda CreateFunction needs iam:PassRole permission.
cards.explanation: iam:PassRole permits the caller to hand that execution role to Lambda. It authorizes passing the role to the service during function creation.

source.title: Grant a user permissions to pass a role to an AWS service

cards.statement: A Lambda function's resource-based policy grants its handler permission to call DynamoDB PutItem.
cards.explanation: A Lambda function receives DynamoDB permissions through its execution role. Its resource-based policy grants other principals access to the function.
cards.misconception: The function's resource-based policy supplies permissions for its handler's DynamoDB calls.

cards.statement: A DynamoDB IAM policy can use dynamodb:LeadingKeys to restrict access by partition key value.
cards.explanation: For supported item operations, dynamodb:LeadingKeys limits requests to permitted partition key values, so a caller can be restricted to its own items.

source.title: Using IAM policy conditions for fine-grained access control
